name: Guyliner / kohl

card.summary: Eyeliner worn by men, from ancient kohl to 2000s emo guyliner; discussed for an intense look, with documented lead concerns about some traditional kohl.
card.note: The FDA considers traditional kohl unsafe because of possible lead content.

quick.overview:
Guyliner is a term for eyeliner worn by men. Kohl, a soft dark powder, is among the oldest eye cosmetics and was worn by Egyptian men and women of all classes. In looksmaxxing talk men's liner is mentioned for a more intense or hunter-eyed look.

No research was found on how liner changes perceived attractiveness in men. The best-documented issue is lead in some traditional kohl.
quick.mechanism: Dark pigment placed along the lash line increases contrast around the eye and can make the eye look larger or more defined. Traditional kohl was made from stibnite or galena; Western products generally use carbon or charcoal.
quick.risks: Studies since the early 1990s have found high lead levels in some kohl products, and lead exposure has been linked to anemia and developmental effects, though some research disputes the links. The FDA does not list kohl as an approved color additive and considers it unsafe, with import and sale in the US illegal. Western commercial eyeliners generally use other pigments.

lead: Kohl is a soft, usually black powder used around the eyes. Traditional kohl was made by grinding stibnite (antimony sulfide), and many modern and homemade versions use galena (lead sulfide); Western manufacturers generally use carbon or charcoal [2]. Egyptians of all social classes are reported to have worn it from about 3100 BCE, and both men and women appear in tomb depictions [1][2].

The term guyliner describes men who wear eyeliner and became popular in the early 2000s emo scene, partly through bands such as Fall Out Boy and Panic! at the Disco [1]. In appearance forums, men's eyeliner is mentioned as a way to look more intense. No studies were found on this effect, while research on lead in some traditional kohl is described below.
infobox: FDA considers kohl unsafe; not an approved color additive

paras: Dark eye lines were used in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia; Wikipedia says possible reasons include shielding skin from sun and warding off the evil eye [1]. Kohl was worn in Egypt from about 3100 BCE, reportedly protecting against eye ailments and glare, and the Arabic word kuhl gave rise to both kohl and alcohol [2]. Lead isotope analysis suggests Nubian populations also used kohl in the Middle Bronze Age [2]. Use spread across North Africa, the Middle East, West Africa and South Asia, with cosmetic, protective and ritual roles [2].

In West Africa kohl is used by both sexes and all ages at weddings and festivals [2]. In the late 20th and early 21st centuries heavy eyeliner became associated with goth, punk and emo styles, and guyliner entered popular usage in the 2000s [1].

In the early 1990s studies found lead levels up to 84% in some commercial kohl samples, and a study about a decade later found lead in about a third of Egyptian and Indian samples [2]. Lead-contaminated kohl has been linked to higher blood lead levels, with possible effects including anemia, developmental delay, lower IQ, seizures and in severe cases death, though some research has disputed these links [2].

The US Food and Drug Administration does not list kohl among approved color additives, considers it unsafe largely because of possible lead content, and says importing or selling it in the US is illegal [2].
No studies found on men's eyeliner and perceived attractiveness. Studies of lead content in kohl and surma are described under safety [2].

timeline.event: The Ebers Papyrus describes kohl as protective for the eyes [2].
Studies report high lead levels in some commercial kohl [2].
Guyliner becomes popular in the emo scene [1].
